Model–paper sessions changing code downstream fall from 113/144 to 54/144, and median time to first scored execution decreases for every model (Figure 5, right).

abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

sections.body: The paper asks whether preserving the procedures and decisions recovered during reproduction improves later reproduction. It defines a four-component refined artifact (refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and reproduction guide) and a construction workflow called ReproBridge. The benchmark has 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, each anchored by five human-verified reference scores. The introduction lists three contributions: the artifact design, the construction workflow, and an empirical evaluation across four coding agents. It reports that refined artifacts improve success by 5.5 to 23.2 pp and reduce downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%. It states that component ablations and human validation of integrity checks are examined later.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Reproduction requires recovering implicit details, and preserving recovered procedures may improve later reproduction by coding agents.

sections.body: A task specifies the data, configuration, procedure, and reporting statistic to reproduce. Each attempt's measurement is modeled as $Y=\mu+D+\varepsilon$, where $D$ is a shift from execution choices that depart from the specified experiment and $\varepsilon$ is zero-mean variation. The selection started from 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, kept 241 with code and non-purely-theoretical content, sampled 50, and retained 36 after exclusions. The curation yields 1,463 tasks, of which 1,029 (70.3%) are numerically compatible and form the downstream set. The compatibility interval is a Student-t prediction interval with a 1% tolerance floor. The section notes that a nearby number alone does not show that the intended experiment was performed.
sections.heading: Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench
sections.headline: Success is judged by whether a new result falls in an interval built from five human-verified reference runs.

sections.body: ReproBridge builds the handoff from a paper and its official repository. Humans define the workflow and delivery standards, while agents perform construction, review, and packaging. The workflow has three stages: Specify fixes the intended experiment before execution, Execute establishes a working procedure and records measurements and failures, and Preserve packages the procedure and its rationale. Six roles carry this work, and a Reviewer tests plans, execution records, and the completed artifact in separate contexts. Each measurement must link to an output file, and delivery requires running the entry points from a clean shell. The guide records ambiguities, change records, and repetition guidance.
sections.heading: ReproBridge: artifact design and construction
sections.headline: Construction records each measurement and repair so that later reproducers can run the handoff without the original conversation.

sections.body: Opus 5 constructs the refined artifacts for the main experiment. Fresh Reproducer sessions attempt all 1,029 tasks from 36 papers with either raw code or a refined artifact. Table 3 reports means over three evaluations: success rose from 72.3% to 91.6% for Sonnet 4.6 and from 67.6% to 90.8% for Gemini 3.8, with gains from 5.5 to 23.2 pp. Tokens fell by 6.3% to 19.8%. Success requires numerical compatibility and no invalidation by an independent Auditor that checks execution evidence. Paper-macro gains, which weight each paper equally, range from 6.7 to 20.7 pp. Harnesses differ across vendors, so cross-model comparisons are descriptive, and refinement does not improve every paper.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Refined artifacts raised success for all four models and cut downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%.

sections.body: PaperBench assesses reconstruction with expert rubrics, and SciReplicate-Bench studies implementation reconstruction. REPRO-Bench and ReplicationBench extend assessment to social science and astrophysics. CORE-Bench tests execution of released capsules and questions about their outputs. PaperCoder constructs repositories through planning and code generation, and AutoReproduce recovers implicit details from cited papers. Reflexion retains verbal feedback, and Voyager accumulates executable skills. A compiler for agent-native research artifacts scores reproduction with a model judge. The authors construct runnable four-component handoffs without evaluation rubrics or human reference scores, and assess them through component removals and an ordinary-outputs control.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Related benchmarks rely on expert rubrics or model judges; this work scores runs against reference intervals and an integrity audit.

sections.body: The primary intended use is a reproducibility check before authors submit a paper and release its artifacts. Executing the specified setup can expose missing details, execution barriers, and paper-code inconsistencies. In one static analysis, 238 in-scope contradiction findings touch 669 distinct selected tasks, but these are neither human-validated error rates nor explanations of measured gains. The evaluation is not a conference-wide reproduction rate. Five reference observations are a protocol choice, not a guarantee of adequate uncertainty estimation. Numerical compatibility does not certify scientific validity, and automated audits miss some violations. API savings concern only downstream sessions, and human time savings require a separate study.
sections.heading: Discussion and limitations
sections.headline: Authors can use ReproBridge before submission, but the evaluation covers retained papers and fixed reference regions only.

sections.body: ReproBridge standardizes recovered reproduction procedures and decisions into four components. ReproBridge-Bench supplies verified reference scores for assessing them. The conclusion states that reproduction success depends jointly on artifact quality and reproducer ability. All four evaluated models reach mean success above 90% with refined artifacts, including those with lower raw-code success. The cross-model success-rate spread and downstream API spending both decrease. Removing code or environment setup causes the largest ablation losses, and removing guides or launchers also reduces success when the other components are retained. Future work should evaluate reuse by human researchers and measure full construction and maintenance costs.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Refined artifacts lifted all four models above 90% mean success, and removing code or environment setup caused the largest losses.

sections.body: Coding agents constructed the refined artifacts, performed downstream reproductions, and produced automated integrity audits. They also assisted human reference reproducers with setup, debugging, and script preparation under human verification. Agent-assisted reviews annotated recovered outcomes and paper-code discrepancies, and these annotations are descriptive rather than causal or human-validated error rates. The authors used generative AI to draft and edit text, write analysis scripts, and prepare figure designs. They defined the research question, benchmark, workflow, and protocols, reviewed all AI-assisted work, and checked reported numbers against recorded results. No synthetic data was generated.
sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.headline: Coding agents built artifacts, ran reproductions and audits, and the authors checked reported numbers against recorded results.

sections.body: Appendix A covers selection and sampling, the human reference protocol, and the statistical rules, including t multipliers of approximately 2.78 and 1.53 for the 95% and 80% intervals. Table 8 gives the research-area assignments used in Figure 1. The 1% tolerance floor is active on 197 retained tasks, and all 21 retained zero-target tasks belong to the higher-variability group. Table 9 lists retained papers with successful task counts from one evaluation. Appendix E gives API cost accounting, including a construction investment of USD 5,026 (USD 139.61 per paper) and the break-even calculation. Figures A2.F7 and A4.F8 show a condensed guide and gains by reference variability.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists selection and sampling rules, the human reference protocol, error model derivations, paper inventories, development results, and cost accounting.
